read.sections.0.heading.source: How a camera matches a face

read.sections.0.text.source: Facial recognition is a kind of AI that tries to tell who a person is from their face. First, the software finds a face in a photo or a video. Then it measures details, such as the distance between the eyes, and turns them into a set of numbers. Next, it compares those numbers with faces stored in a database and gives a score for how alike they are. A phone that opens for your face usually keeps only numbers from your face, not a photo. A search compares one face with many. Either way, a match is a best guess, not proof of who someone is.
read.sections.0.text.back: Facial recognition is a kind of AI that tries to identify who someone is from their face. First, the software looks for a face in a photo or video. Then it measures details, such as the distance between the two eyes, and changes them into a set of numbers. Next, it compares those numbers with faces stored in a database and gives a score for how similar the faces are. A phone that opens for your face usually stores only numbers from your face, not a photo. A search, on the other hand, compares one face with many faces. Whatever the way, a match is a best guess, not proof of who that person is.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Facial recognition is AI that tries to name a person from their face. First, it finds a face in a photo. Then it measures the face, like how far apart the eyes are. It turns this into numbers. Next, it compares the numbers with faces in a database. It scores how alike they are. A phone often keeps only numbers from your face, not a photo. A search checks one face against many. A match is a guess, not proof.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Facial recognition is AI that tries to name someone from their face. First, it looks for a face in a photo. Then it measures that face, such as the distance between the two eyes. It changes this into numbers. Next, it compares the numbers with faces in a database. It gives a score for how similar the faces are. A phone often stores only numbers from your face, not a photo. A search checks one face against many faces. A match is a guess, not proof.

read.sections.1.text.source: Facial recognition has helpful uses. It can open a phone, speed up boarding at some airports and help search for a missing person. But it also brings risks. In 2019, a United States government science agency tested nearly 200 face recognition tools. Many of them wrongly matched two different people far more often for some groups. These included women, older people, children and people of some backgrounds. The best tools made far fewer mistakes. A wrong match could get someone blamed for something they did not do. Cameras can also recognise people from far away, without them knowing, and track where they go. That is a risk to privacy.
read.sections.1.text.back: Facial recognition has helpful uses. It can open a phone, speed up boarding planes at some airports and help look for missing people. But it also brings risks. In 2019, a United States government science agency tested nearly 200 face recognition tools. Many of these tools wrongly matched two different people far more often for some groups. These groups included women, older people, children and people from some backgrounds. The best tools made far fewer mistakes. A wrong match can cause someone to be blamed for something they did not do. Cameras can also recognise people from far away, without them noticing, and track where they go. That is a risk to privacy.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Face cameras can open a phone or help find a missing person. But there are risks too. In 2019, a science group in the United States tested nearly 200 tools. Many made more mistakes for some groups, like women, children and older people. The best tools made fewer mistakes. A wrong match could get someone blamed. Cameras can also track people. They may not know it. This is a risk to privacy.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Face cameras can open a phone or help look for missing people. But there are also risks. In 2019, a science group in the United States tested nearly 200 tools. Many tools made more mistakes for some groups, such as women, children and older people. The best tools made fewer mistakes. A wrong match can cause someone to be blamed. Cameras can also track people. They may not know. This is a risk to privacy.

read.sections.2.text.source: Because of these risks, places make different choices. In 2019, San Francisco became the first city in the United States to ban facial recognition by its police and other city offices. Since 2025, a European Union law has banned some uses. Police may not use live facial recognition in public places, except in a few serious cases, such as a search for a missing person. A judge or an independent official must agree first. The law also bans copying face photos in bulk from the internet or security cameras to build a face recognition database. Ordinary cameras are not banned, and other places allow much wider use.
read.sections.2.text.back: Because of these risks, each place makes different choices. In 2019, San Francisco became the first city in the United States to ban facial recognition by the police and other city offices. Since 2025, a European Union law has banned some uses. The police may not use live facial recognition in public places, except in a few serious cases, such as looking for a missing person. A judge or an independent official must agree first. That law also bans copying face photos on a large scale from the internet or security cameras to build a facial recognition database. Ordinary cameras are not banned, and other places allow far wider use.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: In 2019, San Francisco made a ban. Its police may not use facial recognition. The European Union has an AI law. Police there may not use live face cameras in public. A few serious cases are allowed, like a search for a lost person. A judge or an official must say yes. The law also bans copying lots of face photos online for a face database. Normal cameras are not banned.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: In 2019, San Francisco made a ban. Its police may not use facial recognition. The European Union has an AI law. The police there may not use face cameras live in public places. A few serious cases are allowed, such as looking for a missing person. A judge or an official must agree. That law also bans copying many face photos online for a face database. Ordinary cameras are not banned.

watch.summary.source: In this video, a reporter talks with an expert in computer vision who is also a lawyer. Facial recognition is used to open phones, name friends in photos and help people board planes. It works by finding patterns in faces. To learn them, it needs many photos, sometimes millions, with labels that say who is in them. Police see a benefit. They can search many photos quickly, and that matters in serious cases. But the expert names two kinds of worry. If the tool is wrong, it may name the wrong person. Research found it works worse for some groups. If the tool is right, people could be watched and tracked without knowing. Some cities in the United States, such as San Francisco, banned government use. The expert says people should decide together how it is used.
watch.summary.back: In this video, a reporter talks with an expert in computer vision who is also a lawyer. Facial recognition is used to open phones, name friends in photos and help people board planes. It works by looking for patterns in faces. To learn them, it needs many photos, sometimes millions, with labels that say who is in the photo. The police see its benefit. They can search through many photos quickly, and that matters in serious cases. But the expert mentions two kinds of worry. If the tool is wrong, it may name the wrong person. Research found it works worse for some groups. If the tool is right, people can be watched and tracked without them noticing. Some cities in the United States, such as San Francisco, banned its use by the government. The expert says people should decide together how it is used.

educatorNotes.0.source: The Greenport cases, the test numbers (12 wrong matches in 1,000) and the activity sentences are made up. The real facts, simplified: NIST tested 189 mostly commercial algorithms from 99 developers in 2019 and found false matches often 10 to over 100 times more frequent for some groups, varying by algorithm, with the most accurate showing smaller differences. Phones: Apple's security guide says Face ID saves mathematical representations of the face, not images, and they never leave the device; other phones differ. EU AI Act, Article 5, applying since 2 February 2025: police use of real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces is banned except where strictly necessary to search for victims of abduction or trafficking or missing persons, to prevent a specific and imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack, or to find suspects of listed serious crimes (at least four years in prison); each use needs prior authorisation by a judicial or independent administrative authority (in an emergency, within 24 hours), and only where national law allows it. Identifying people later from recordings is not banned but is high-risk, with stricter duties due to apply later (the Commission's page gives 2 December 2027 as of November 2026). The scraping ban covers AI systems that build or expand facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV; it does not ban every use of a face photo found online. Rules change: check them before teaching. Lesson 8 (bias from missing training data) is a good link. Paper version of the activity: write the eight sentences on cards and sort them into the three groups; reward reasons, not the group, and accept "yes with rules" when the learner explains the rules.
educatorNotes.0.back: The Greenport cases, the test figures (12 wrong matches out of 1,000) and the activity sentences are made up. The real facts, briefly: NIST tested 189 algorithms, mostly commercial, from 99 developers in 2019 and found false matches often 10 to over 100 times more frequent for some groups, varying by algorithm, with the most accurate showing smaller differences. Phones: Apple's security guide states that Face ID stores mathematical representations of the face, not images, and they never leave the device; other phones differ. EU AI Act, Article 5, applying since 2 February 2025: police use of real-time remote biometric identification in spaces accessible to the public is banned except where strictly necessary to search for victims of kidnapping or human trafficking or missing persons, to prevent a specific and imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack, or to find suspects of listed serious crimes (at least four years in prison); each use needs prior permission from a judicial or independent administrative authority (in an emergency, within 24 hours), and only where national law allows it. Identifying people later from recordings is not banned but is high-risk, with stricter duties to apply later (the Commission's page gives the date 2 December 2027 as of November 2026). The scraping ban covers AI systems that build or expand facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV; it does not ban every use of a face photo found online. Rules change: check before teaching. Lesson 8 (bias from training data left out) is a good link. Paper version of the activity: write the eight sentences on cards and sort them into three groups; value the reasons, not the group, and accept "yes with rules" when the learner explains the rules.
